title: Parashurama's challenge
hook: on the road home from the wedding, a man with an axe stops Rama: one avatar of Vishnu meets the next
carry: avatara: the divine comes down, again and again

segments.voice: Yesterday: four couples circled one fire, and Janaka gave Sita to Rama as sahadharmachari, his companion in dharma.

It should be a caravan of pure joy. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly. At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. A wind rises. The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.
screen: `A CARAVAN OF PURE JOY.` → `BAD BIRDS, GOOD DEER.` → `A MAN WITH AN AXE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, the axe across his shoulder. He's the son of the sage Jamadagni, of the family of Bhrigu, a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons. After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe. Now he has heard that a young prince broke Shiva's great bow, so he's brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two bows, one for Shiva and one for Vishnu. In his telling, a contest broke out, and one roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack. Shiva's bow passed to the kings of Videha; that's the one Rama broke. Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's family, and here it is. String this one, he tells Rama, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs; Parashurama doesn't even answer him. Here is what Hindus see on this road. The word is avatara, a coming down. Hindus count ten great descents of Vishnu, the Dashavatara, and in most lists Parashurama is the sixth and Rama the seventh. Why come down at all? In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, another avatar, gives the reason: whenever dharma falls and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. So on a dusty road home from a wedding, one Rama faces another, and in the tradition's eyes, both are Vishnu.
screen: `A FIRE NO ONE CAN LOOK AT.` · `TWO BOWS: SHIVA'S AND VISHNU'S.` · `STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.` · `AVATARA: A COMING DOWN.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA FALLS, I COME.` · then, large: `ONE AVATAR MEETS THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say softly on each breath out, om namo narayanaya, a prayer to Vishnu, the one who keeps coming down when he's needed. Let the words slow you. If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and picture the wedding party on that road, everyone still, waiting to see what the young prince will do.
Parashurama's challenge. Rama with the axe, counted the sixth avatar, meets Rama the seventh and holds out Vishnu's bow: string it, and then we fight.
Your line: avatara, the divine comes down, again and again. Tomorrow, Rama answers. That's day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition counts Parashurama among Vishnu's ten avatars, the Dashavatara, usually listed sixth after the man-lion and the dwarf and before Rama; his birth is marked on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

original.note: Sanskrit paraśurāma: Rama with the paraśu, the axe. Valmiki mostly calls him Jamadagnya, son of Jamadagni.

Parashurama.meaning: Rama with the axe; later tradition counts him an avatar of Vishnu

Bhrigu.meaning: an ancient sage whose family Parashurama belongs to

Videha.meaning: Janaka's kingdom, where Shiva's bow was kept

avatars.meaning: forms in which Vishnu comes down to earth

Dashavatara.meaning: the ten great descents of Vishnu

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; the Baroda critical edition differs. Please confirm.
Valmiki mostly names him Jamadagnya or Bhargava Rama; the name Parashurama is used here as the index does. Confirm framing as 'later tradition calls him'.
The contest of the two bows: the script says Vishnu's roar (humkara) made Shiva's bow slack. Confirm detail.
Avatar lists vary; 'usually sixth' is softened deliberately.
The story of his war on the kshatriyas is given only in outline (no count of twenty-one times).
Reviewer: 'a king killed his father' softened to 'killed in a feud with a royal house'; traditions differ on whether Kartavirya Arjuna or his sons killed Jamadagni. Confirm.

Reviewer: the bow contest ranks Vishnu over Shiva. It is in Valmiki (Bala 75), but Shaiva listeners may hear it as sectarian; the script now frames it as Parashurama's telling. A Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to Shaiva traditions.
